## Research question and scope

This notebook asks: **After a luckier H-1B lottery year, do firms apply for
more or fewer H-1B visas in the following year, and does this relationship vary
across industries?** It builds directly on the lottery-luck and next-year
participation analysis, with industry-specific estimates as an exploratory
extension.

The next-year participation outcomes are observed for the full H-1B employer
panel. Industry, however, is available only when an employer links to
Compustat. Since Compustat covers public firms, all industry-specific results
are limited to this Compustat-matched public-firm subset. They should not be
read as describing the industry composition or responses of all H-1B employers.

Throughout, “lottery luck” is the firm's selection shock: actual selections
minus the number expected from the national selection rate in that lottery
year. The estimates are exploratory heterogeneity results, not proof that the
causal response differs across industries.

## Load saved data

```{r}
#| label: packages-and-paths

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
library(fixest)
library(broom)
library(knitr)

options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

# Load the saved analysis files from the project's data folder. The fallback
# supports older checkouts that stored the same files at the project root; no
# raw data are read or reconstructed in this notebook.
locate_saved_file <- function(filename) {
  candidates <- c(file.path("data", filename), filename)
  existing <- candidates[file.exists(candidates)]
  if (length(existing) == 0) {
    stop("Could not find saved derived input: ", filename, call. = FALSE)
  }
  existing[[1]]
}

participation_path <- locate_saved_file("h1b_lottery_participation_panel.rds")
firm_year_path <- locate_saved_file("h1b_firm_year_analysis.rds")

# The participation panel supplies the next-year outcomes. The firm-year panel
# is used only to attach the prepared broad-industry label and match indicator.
participation <- readRDS(participation_path)
firm_year <- readRDS(firm_year_path) |>
  select(ein, lottery_year, sector, compustat_ein_match)

required_participation_variables <- c(
  "ein", "lottery_year", "n_registrations", "selection_shock",
  "selection_luck_10pp", "next_year_registrations", "returns_next_year",
  "log_current_registrations", "log_next_year_registrations"
)
stopifnot(all(required_participation_variables %in% names(participation)))
```

## Full-panel participation and industry coverage

The first table is intentionally based on the full participation panel. It
shows the scale of the main analysis before restricting to the public-firm
sample needed to observe industry. The second table reports which industries
are available after that restriction.

```{r}
#| label: full-panel-summary

full_participation_summary <- participation |>
  summarise(
    firm_years = n(), firms = n_distinct(ein),
    current_registrations = sum(n_registrations),
    next_year_registrations = sum(next_year_registrations),
    returns_next_year_rate = mean(returns_next_year)
  )

full_participation_summary |>
  mutate(returns_next_year_rate = scales::percent(returns_next_year_rate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(caption = "Next-year participation panel: full H-1B employer sample")

industry_panel <- participation |>
  left_join(firm_year, by = c("ein", "lottery_year"))

industry_coverage <- industry_panel |>
  mutate(industry_coverage = case_when(
    compustat_ein_match & !is.na(sector) & sector != "Unknown" ~ sector,
    compustat_ein_match ~ "Matched, industry unavailable",
    TRUE ~ "Not matched to Compustat"
  )) |>
  group_by(industry_coverage) |>
  summarise(
    firm_years = n(), firms = n_distinct(ein),
    current_registrations = sum(n_registrations),
    next_year_registrations = sum(next_year_registrations),
    returns_next_year_rate = mean(returns_next_year), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(firm_years))

industry_coverage |>
  mutate(returns_next_year_rate = scales::percent(returns_next_year_rate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(digits = 0, caption = "Industry availability and next-year participation")
```

## Descriptive participation by industry

These summaries use only Compustat-matched firms with a recorded broad
industry. The registration measures are counts, because the question is whether
firms submit more or fewer registrations in the next lottery year—not
employee-scaled exposure.

```{r}
#| label: industry-descriptives

industry_sample <- industry_panel |>
  filter(compustat_ein_match, !is.na(sector), sector != "Unknown")

industry_descriptives <- industry_sample |>
  group_by(sector) |>
  summarise(
    firm_years = n(), firms = n_distinct(ein),
    current_registrations = sum(n_registrations),
    next_year_registrations = sum(next_year_registrations),
    mean_current_registrations = mean(n_registrations),
    mean_next_year_registrations = mean(next_year_registrations),
    return_rate = mean(returns_next_year),
    mean_selection_shock = mean(selection_shock), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(current_registrations))

industry_descriptives |>
  mutate(return_rate = scales::percent(return_rate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Descriptive next-year participation by industry")
```

## Lottery-luck models by industry

The primary outcome is `log(1 + next-year registrations)`, which captures
whether a firm applies for more or fewer visas while retaining firms with zero
registrations next year. As a complementary extensive-margin outcome, the
notebook also estimates whether a firm returns to the lottery at all.

For each industry, the exploratory reduced-form specification is:

\[
Y_{i,t+1} = \beta_s\,\text{lottery luck}_{it} +
\gamma\log(1 + \text{current registrations}_{it}) +
\text{lottery-year fixed effects} + e_{it}.
\]

Lottery luck is expressed as the firm's selection-rate surprise in 10
percentage-point units (`selection_luck_10pp`). Standard errors are clustered
by firm EIN. The current-registration control compares firms with similar
current H-1B application scale. Sector-specific comparisons remain exploratory.

To avoid reporting extremely small industry cells, a model is shown only if it
has at least **50 usable firm-years** after all model variables are observed.
This is a reporting threshold, not a claim that every reported estimate is
precise.

```{r}
#| label: model-sample-sizes

minimum_usable_firm_years <- 50L
outcomes <- c(
  log_next_year_registrations = "Log(1 + next-year registrations)",
  returns_next_year = "Returns to lottery next year"
)

model_ready_counts <- bind_rows(lapply(names(outcomes), function(outcome_name) {
  industry_sample |>
    filter(!is.na(.data[[outcome_name]]), !is.na(selection_luck_10pp),
      !is.na(log_current_registrations)) |>
    group_by(sector) |>
    summarise(usable_firm_years = n(), usable_firms = n_distinct(ein),
      .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(outcome = outcomes[[outcome_name]])
}))

model_ready_counts |>
  arrange(outcome, desc(usable_firm_years)) |>
  kable(caption = "Usable observations by industry and outcome")
```

```{r}
#| label: estimate-industry-models

estimate_industry_model <- function(data, outcome_name, outcome_label) {
  estimation_data <- data |>
    filter(!is.na(.data[[outcome_name]]), !is.na(selection_luck_10pp),
      !is.na(log_current_registrations))
  eligible_industries <- estimation_data |>
    count(sector, name = "n") |>
    filter(n >= minimum_usable_firm_years) |>
    pull(sector)

  bind_rows(lapply(eligible_industries, function(industry_name) {
    industry_data <- filter(estimation_data, sector == industry_name)
    model <- feols(
      as.formula(paste0(outcome_name,
        " ~ selection_luck_10pp + log_current_registrations | lottery_year")),
      data = industry_data, cluster = ~ein
    )
    luck_term <- tidy(model) |> filter(term == "selection_luck_10pp")
    tibble(
      outcome = outcome_label, industry = industry_name,
      firm_years = nobs(model), firms = n_distinct(industry_data$ein),
      luck_coefficient = luck_term$estimate, std_error = luck_term$std.error,
      conf_low = luck_term$estimate - 1.96 * luck_term$std.error,
      conf_high = luck_term$estimate + 1.96 * luck_term$std.error,
      p_value = luck_term$p.value
    )
  }))
}

industry_model_results <- bind_rows(lapply(names(outcomes), function(outcome_name) {
  estimate_industry_model(industry_sample, outcome_name, outcomes[[outcome_name]])
})) |>
  arrange(outcome, desc(luck_coefficient))

industry_model_results |>
  mutate(across(c(luck_coefficient, std_error, conf_low, conf_high), ~ round(.x, 3)),
    p_value = signif(p_value, 3)) |>
  kable(caption = paste0("Industry-specific lottery-luck estimates; industries require at least ",
    minimum_usable_firm_years, " usable firm-years"))
```

```{r}
#| label: industry-coefficient-plot
#| fig-cap: "Exploratory lottery-luck estimates by industry, with 95% confidence intervals"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

coefficient_plot <- ggplot(industry_model_results,
  aes(x = luck_coefficient, y = reorder(industry, luck_coefficient))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey55", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf_low, xmax = conf_high), height = 0.18) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, color = "#2166AC") +
  facet_wrap(~outcome, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Coefficient on lottery luck (10 percentage-point selection-rate surprise)", y = NULL)

print(coefficient_plot)
```

## Interpretation and next steps

Start with the full-panel result from the core lottery-luck notebook, then use
the table and plot here to ask whether the *point estimates* look larger or
smaller in particular public-firm industries. Give the greatest weight to
industries with enough firms and narrow confidence intervals. Differences in
point estimates alone are not evidence of a causal industry difference,
particularly where intervals overlap or industry samples are small.

The next education-level heterogeneity analysis should use the same next-year
participation outcomes and lottery-luck definition, state clearly that degree
data describe approved petitions rather than all lottery applicants, and avoid
claiming degree-specific causal effects without degree-specific lottery
variation.
